title_original: Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall Commission Is No Spectacle. Thank Goodness
excerpt_original: Musicians have been invited to respond to his unusual installation-turned-instrument.

blocks.text: Walking into Tate Modern ‘s Turbine Hall on Monday morning, I experienced an initial wave of disappointment. The latest commission for the space, by Tarek Atoui , is certainly no spectacle. The hovering assemblage of bamboo frames, instruments, and draped electrical wires—all in a subtle color scheme of gray, beige, and orange—looks a bit like a cross between a boiler room and a mid-tier design store.

However, if the installation, Hold , lacks the immediate wow factor of some of its predecessors, it proffers instead a new way of experiencing the cavernous, post-industrial space.

The environment is filled with instruments, including Korean drums, Uzbek horns, gongs, and shengs, strung up beside glowing, amber-toned lights. Large slabs of stone litter the ground, providing spots for visitors to sit. D.J. equipment covers one long, altar-like surface toward the back of the room.

blocks.alt: an installation of bamboo sticks, instruments, and hanging lightbulbs in a very large exhibition space

blocks.text: Installation view of Tarek Atoui’s commission at Tate Modern, 2026. Photo: Susan Davis.

The surrounding space reverberated with sound on my visit: at one time with a deep, bellowing thrum, and later with a more melodic tinkle. At one point, the proud, yawning call of a horn unfurled at its leisure. It is a sound you can imagine commanding attention at any time in human history. The music is ever-changing, generated by a complex computer program crafted by Atoui.

The Lebanese artist, who lives in Paris, sees the installation as a culmination of two decades of musical collaborations. “Each instrument has a history, has a story,” he said at a press preview for the show.

But it is also a starting point of sorts. He has asked several musicians to respond to the space in a series of live sessions , which kick off this week with Mazen Kerbaj , Kenichi Iwasa , and Aya Metwalli . There will also be a program of workshops.

“It’s not an easy space to tame,” Atoui said, explaining that he picked performers he believes will be sensitive to its quirks. Sufficiently curious practitioners will be able to “play the whole space like an instrument,” he said.

blocks.alt: an installation of bamboo sticks, instruments, and hanging lightbulbs in a very large exhibition space

blocks.text: Installation view of Tarek Atoui’s commission at Tate Modern, 2026. Photo: Susan Davis.

The Turbine Hall is a commission that many in the art world love to hate. In the wake of so many failed wannabe showstoppers, including last year’s much-criticized tribute to Sámi ancestral knowledge, the vast space might strike a new artist as overpowering, rather than inviting. I always hope to encounter something able to fill the venue and redefine it.

Atoui achieves this, but not in a way we’ve seen before. He conjures sculpture out of sound and, still more intangibly, asks us to gather, mingle, and improvise our own sounds in response. If this vision comes together as he describes it, his creation may prove surprisingly memorable.
“Tarek Atoui: Hold” is on view through April 11, 2027 in the Turbine Hall at Tate Modern.
